cards.front: Why is night driving riskier, and when must your headlamps be on?
cards.back: Night driving runs far deadlier with weaker sight, so daylight trips beat night runs and tired drivers stay parked, night speeds drop inside headlight range, lamps burn from thirty minutes after sunset to thirty minutes before sunrise or under one-thousand-foot visibility, and eyes shift low-right against oncoming glare.

cards.front: When must you switch to low beams?
cards.back: Low beams take over within five hundred feet of oncoming cars, within three hundred feet behind leaders, on lit roads, and in fog, rain, sleet, snow, or dust, while night-parked cars on dark highways keep parking or low beams lit.

cards.front: What times and visibility turn headlights on, and how close to other cars do you dip to low beams?
cards.back: Use headlights from a half-hour after sunset to a half-hour before sunrise, or whenever people or vehicles cannot be seen clearly for at least one thousand feet. Use low beams within five hundred feet of an approaching vehicle or when following another vehicle within three hundred feet.
cards.memory_hook: five hundred ahead, three hundred behind

cards.front: How should you plan a highway trip and enter a highway?
cards.back: Texas highways span the maintained public width between boundary lines, trips pre-plan entrances, directions, and exits with fit drivers and cars skipping roads above their minimum pace, and entries yield to highway traffic through right-side speed-change lanes with left signals and merging speed.

cards.front: What are the steps for entering a highway?
cards.back: Highway entries yield to flow, ride right-side speed lanes, signal left, and accelerate into merges.

cards.front: Which highway lanes are for slower and faster traffic, and what gaps should you keep?
cards.back: Highway lanes assign right to minimum-or-slower pace, middle and left to faster travel and passing, and early exits to prompt lane moves, then demand centered steady pacing without weaving, two-second gaps stretching to four in weather with sudden-stop readiness, merger room, and faster-traffic passing room from non-right lanes.

cards.front: How should you prepare to exit a highway?
cards.back: Exits claim their lane early and earlier in heavy traffic with signs posted at least one thousand yards out, then slow along ramps into the lower limit.

cards.front: What are the roles of the right, middle, and left highway lanes, and how early are exits signed?
cards.back: Use the right freeway lane for the minimum posted speed or speeds below traffic flow, and middle or left lanes for faster travel or passing. Move into the exit lane early; exit signs are usually at least one thousand yards before the exit.
cards.memory_hook: Usually at least one thousand yards

cards.front: How do you fight highway hypnosis, and what phone rules apply?
cards.back: Highway hypnosis from drone and monotony yields to stops every two hours or one hundred miles with walks, eight-hour driving days, roaming eyes on signs and mirrors, open-window air, daytime-only sunglasses, blind-spot avoidance by hanging back or passing through, and phones parked for pull-overs or hands-free use with under-eighteen use banned outside emergencies.

cards.front: What gaps, break intervals, and daily driving limits does the handbook give for highway trips?
cards.back: Gaps hold two seconds dry and four seconds foul, trips break every two hours or one hundred miles, and days cap at eight hours.

cards.front: What should you do if your vehicle breaks down?
cards.back: Breakdowns move everyone off roads that trap cars with warning devices out, roll stricken cars off pavement even on flats, flash emergency and tail lamps plus cabin lights at night, and fly white cloths or raised hoods.

cards.front: In what order do you handle a breakdown?
cards.back: Breakdowns empty people first, then cars, then light everything, then signal distress with cloth or hood.

cards.front: How should you handle a skid, and how can you prevent one?
cards.back: Every emergency obeys think-before-you-act, so skids meet lifted gas pedals instead of slammed brakes, steering into the slide, and gentle straightening, with prevention via slower poor-condition driving and sound-tread tires.

cards.front: How do you handle brake failure, running off the pavement, a blowout, or a steep descent?
cards.back: Brake failure answers with calm parking-brake plus lower-gear slowing short of lockup, pavement departures answer with gripped wheels, lifted gas, careful braking, and slowed checked re-entry, flats and blowouts answer with lifted gas, gentle brakes, and straight stops, and steep descents answer with low gears and never neutral or clutch coasting.

cards.front: What do the responses to skids, brake failure, run-offs, and flats have in common?
cards.back: Skids steer into slides, brake failures ease parking brakes with low gears, departures slow before re-entering, and flats stop straight, all without slammed brakes.

cards.front: How should you drive on snow and ice?
cards.back: Winter widen gaps against icy rear-enders since snow tires still slide, admits no safe snow-or-ice speed, bans brake-locking, clears windows with working wipers and defrosters, suspects bridge ice, shady melt delays, and turns, starts gently with brake tests and pre-turn slowing, and trusts chains most while denying them normal-speed security.

cards.front: Which winter rules about speed, chains, bridges, and shade does the handbook stress?
cards.back: Winter admits no safe speed and no trustworthy chains, suspects bridges and shade first, and starts and stops gently.

cards.front: How does a modern roundabout work, and how do you drive one?
cards.back: Modern roundabouts circle one-way counterclockwise under yield signs with eight conflict points against thirty-two at signalized four-ways, driven by slowing, yielding to circling traffic, counterclockwise entry, and signaled right exits, with single lanes heeding advisory speeds and bike-or-pedestrian crossings, multi-lanes obeying advance lane signs without in-circle changes, big rigs granted room, and emergency pull-overs kept to approaches and exits rather than inside.

cards.front: What are the key steps for driving through a roundabout?
cards.back: Roundabouts yield to circling traffic, loop counterclockwise, exit right with signals, and never halt inside for sirens.

cards.front: How do floodwater depths affect a vehicle, and what should you do?
cards.back: Nearly half of flash-flood deaths involve vehicles. Six inches reaches the underside of most passenger cars, causing lost control and possible stalling; twelve inches floats many cars. Two feet of rushing water can sweep away pickups, SUVs and most other vehicles. Floodwater may conceal missing roadbed or a bridge, and weakened roads may collapse under a vehicle after water recedes. Leave a stalled vehicle quickly for higher ground; avoid flooded routes by choosing another way. A vehicle floats when buoyancy exceeds its weight. Modern roundabouts reduce severe intersection crashes by an average of eighty percent.

cards.front: What happens at six inches, twelve inches, and two feet of moving water?
cards.back: Six inches of water steals control, twelve inches floats cars, and two rushing feet carry trucks, so drowned routes turn around.

cards.front: How do trucks differ from cars, and how should you pass one?
cards.back: Trucks brake and accelerate slower, swing wider, and weigh more, so passes check fronts, rears, mirrors, and blind spots for clear legal zones, flash headlights especially at night while trucks hold far sides, budget three to five extra seconds level with easier climbs and harder descents, finish fast without lingering, and return only on truck light-flashes with full truck fronts mirrored while holding speed.

cards.front: How much extra time does a truck pass take, and when may you return in front?
cards.back: Truck passes cost three to five extra seconds with headlight flashes, and returns wait for flashed clearance plus full truck fronts in mirrors.

cards.front: What should you do when a truck passes you, when you meet one, and when you follow one?
cards.back: Passed drivers drift far-side, ease speed, never accelerate, and heed truck return signals, oncoming meetings hug far sides against sideswipes since turbulence pushes apart, following respects two-hundred-forty-foot car stops against four-hundred-plus-foot loaded rig stops at fifty-five miles per hour, rear blind spots stay empty with drivers visible in truck side mirrors, night lights dim against mirror glare, and uphill stops leave rollback room on the left for visibility.

cards.front: How do car and loaded-rig stopping distances compare, and what does a truck's mirror tell you?
cards.back: Cars stop near two hundred forty feet while loaded rigs need four hundred plus, unseen drivers mean unseen cars, and turbulence pushes apart.

cards.front: What should you watch for when trucks turn right, back up, or are cut off?
cards.back: Truck right turns swing wide past deceptive right-side gaps that passing cars must avoid, backing trucks block roads that waiting cars must respect from outside blind spots, center-lane cruising aids merges and escape options, cutoffs steal safety cushions with construction-zone races worst of all, and big size masks true truck speed at intersections.

cards.front: Why are motorcyclists hard to see, and what crash is most deadly for them?
cards.back: Motorcyclists share full road rights, yet half of bike crashes involve other vehicles and riders die about thirty-five times more often, hidden by car-seeking eyes, tiny profiles, tricky distance judgment, constant lane shifts, and distraction, with left turns across their path most deadly plus blind spots, surface hazards, wind gusts, and large-vehicle blocking.

cards.front: How should you drive around motorcycles at intersections and when changing lanes?
cards.back: Bike-aware drivers double-check intersections especially before lefts, signal every lane move since bike signals rarely self-cancel and flashing liars must prove their turns, and grant full lane widths without sharing.

cards.front: What are the biggest motorcycle dangers, and what protects riders?
cards.back: The most common car-motorcycle collision is a car turning left in front of a motorcycle at an intersection. Motorcyclists are often hidden in blind spots; check mirrors and blind spots before lane changes and at intersections, signal before changing lanes or merging, and allow a motorcycle its full lane width.

cards.front: How far should you follow a motorcycle, and what light rail rules apply?
cards.back: Followers trail bikes four to six seconds back and a full car length at stops against rear-end shoves, remembering dry bikes outbrake cars, while the training program born in nineteen eighty-three and moved from DPS to licensing regulators in twenty twenty spends fee money on rider skills, and quiet street light rail demands never occupying tracks, crossing only designated spots both ways under all signals, listening for horns and bells, and never racing, beating, or circling gates.

cards.front: What rights do bicycles have, and what crashes are most common?
cards.back: Bicycles count as vehicles with full rights and duties, ride beyond right lanes on one-way multi-lane streets and car-pathed left turns, earn motorist merges on right turns without cut-across moves, hug right only in safely shareable lanes, claim full lanes to pass, turn left, dodge hazards, or survive narrow lanes, and crash most when cars left-hook oncoming riders, right-hook their paths, or pull from stops across their right-of-way.

cards.front: What following gap, rail rule, and lane rule protect bikes and rail crossings?
cards.back: Follow a motorcycle with at least a four-to-six-second gap. Do not drive, stop or park on light-rail tracks; cross only at designated crossings when safe. A bicyclist may take a full lane to pass, prepare a left turn, avoid hazards or when side-by-side sharing is unsafe in a narrow lane. Watch for right-turn and intersection conflicts.
cards.memory_hook: Designated safe crossings and rider space

cards.front: What is distracted driving, and how can you prevent it?
cards.back: Distraction steals eyes, hands, or minds from driving until gazes miss plain sights, triggered by texting, passengers, stereos, food, reading, retrievals, billboards, gawking, phones, telematics, and daydreams, doubling crashes on half-second delays, fought by pre-learning devices, pre-setting stations and media, decluttering, pre-planning routes, pre-setting mirrors, banning in-motion reading and texting, skipping smoke and meals, and cooling intense talks, while others' drifting, speed swings, object fumbling, and chatting earn extra room and careful passes.

cards.front: What does the Texas texting law ban, and which calls are allowed?
cards.back: Texting law bans reading, writing, and sending on portable wireless devices with fines on conviction, ignores ringing phones, allows law-enforcement and emergency calls, and otherwise pulls cars off roads for short or passenger-placed calls.

cards.front: How much do half-second delays raise crash risk, and what phone use is still allowed?
cards.back: Half-second delays double crashes, and texting bans all reading, writing, and sending outside law and emergency calls.

recap_hooks.text: Headlamps go on from thirty minutes after sunset to thirty minutes before sunrise.
Dip to low beams within five hundred feet of oncoming cars and three hundred feet behind.
Enter highways through the speed-change lane, signal left, and merge at speed.
Keep right if slower; use middle and left lanes to pass.
Move into the exit lane early, and slow on the ramp.
Stop every two hours or one hundred miles.
In a breakdown, get people off the road, then the car, then turn on lights.
In a skid, lift off the gas and steer into the slide.
Never coast downhill in neutral.
There is no safe speed on snow or ice; bridges and shade ice first.
In a roundabout, yield to circling traffic and travel counterclockwise.
Turn Around Don't Drown: twelve inches of water can float a car.
Trucks brake slower and swing wider; pass with room and return only with the full truck front in your mirror.
If you cannot see a truck's mirrors, the driver cannot see you.
Never cut off a truck or pass on the right of a turning truck.
Motorcyclists have full road rights; double-check for them before left turns.
Follow motorcycles four to six seconds back, and never stop on light rail tracks.
Bicycles are vehicles with full rights and duties.
Distraction takes your eyes, hands, or mind off driving.
Texas bans reading, writing, and sending on portable devices while driving.
